raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old man with history of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency underwent orthotopic liver transplant. His postoperative course was complicated by an incarcerated inguinal hernia that was repaired uneventfully and cytomegalovirus (CMV) viremia that was treated with valganciclovir. He was discharged on maintenance immunosuppression of mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and prednisone. He then presented 5 weeks post-transplant with 2 days of encephalopathy and increasing home oxygen requirements. On arrival, he required 4L nasal cannula to maintain oxygen saturation >92% and encephalopathy characterized by sparse speech and disorientation with a nonfocal neurologic examination. Other vital signs and physical examination were within normal limits. His white blood cell count was 9.3 x 109/L, creatinine 2.12 mg/dL (baseline <1.0 mg/dL) and blood urea nitrogen of 53 mg/dL (baseline <20 mg/dL). His synthetic liver function international normalized ratio, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and bilirubin were within normal limits. His arterial ammonia was unusually elevated at 204 micromol/L in the emergency department precipitating an intensive care unit (ICU) admission. Induction dosing of intravenous ganciclovir was started for elevated CMV titers. He was started on empiric antibiotic coverage with vancomycin, meropenem, micafungin after blood cultures were drawn. Intravenous micronutrient supplementation for B1, B6, and levocarnitine was initiated on admission to the ICU. Lumbar puncture on admission revealed an opening pressure of 8 cmH2O, but Gram stain revealed encapsulated yeast suspicious for Cryptococcus. He was started on liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine. For his hyperammonemia, he was started on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and rifaximin, zinc, and lactulose. Ammonia proceeded to unexpectedly climb to 692 micromol/L over the ensuing 12 to 24 hours with concomitant neurological deterioration necessitating mechanical ventilation. Empiric intravenous doxycycline was started after a urine and bronchial aspirate was obtained for Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Forty-eight hours after antifungal induction and CRRT, ammonia levels had fallen to <100 micromol/L (see Figure 1). Cryptococcal serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) antigen titers both returned positive at >1:2560. Cultures from bronchoalveolar lavage, CSF, and blood all revealed cryptococcal growth consistent with disseminated disease.
Repeat lumbar punctures revealed opening pressures greater than 45 cmH2O requiring large volume drainage every 48 hours. Unfortunately, permanent CSF diversion was not possible given persistent thrombocytopenia that developed 48 hours into his hospitalization reaching a nadir of 16 x 103/microL. His mental status transiently improved, but he was unable to wean from mechanical ventilation and ultimately require tracheostomy. Even after culture clearance, he continued to display complications of cryptococcal infection related to sludging and obstruction of microvascular structures, resulting in persistent hydrocephalus, oliguric renal failure, and progressive splenic infarcts with necrosis requiring splenectomy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain did not reveal cytotoxic edema which was likely prevented by the rapid correction of ammonia levels. His hospital course was further complicated by sepsis, duodenal leak, persisting renal failure, and failure to thrive. Given poor quality of life with multiple unresolved end-organ problems, the family decided to move to comfort care in hospice. Urea cycle disorder screening studies eventually returned revealing a low urine orotic level and a normal serum citrulline and arginine level making this diagnosis unlikely.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old male orthotopic liver transplant recipient presented 5 weeks post-transplant with a 2-day history of encephalopathy and increasing home oxygen requirements.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Five weeks after undergoing orthotopic liver transplantation for NASH and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (complicated postoperatively by an incarcerated inguinal hernia repair and CMV viremia treated with valganciclovir), the patient presented with 2 days of progressive disorientation, sparse speech, and worsening hypoxemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Cirrhosis secondary to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency status post orthotopic liver transplantation 5 weeks prior; postoperative incarcerated inguinal hernia repair and CMV viremia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for disorientation, sparse speech, and increasing supplemental oxygen requirement. Home medications: mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, prednisone, and valganciclovir.

objective.physical_examination: Required 4 L/min nasal cannula oxygen to maintain SpO2 >92%, sparse speech, disorientation, and a nonfocal neurological examination (rapidly deteriorating within 24 hours to coma requiring mechanical ventilation and eventual tracheostomy).
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 9.3 x 10^9/L, acute kidney injury with creatinine 2.12 mg/dL (baseline <1.0 mg/dL) and BUN 53 mg/dL (baseline <20 mg/dL), normal synthetic liver function and LFTs (INR, ALT, AST, bilirubin), elevated CMV viral load, severe hyperammonemia with arterial ammonia 204 umol/L on arrival (climbing to 692 umol/L within 12-24 hours before dropping to <100 umol/L after 48 hours of CRRT and antifungals), severe thrombocytopenia reaching a nadir of 16 x 10^3/uL, and normal urea cycle disorder screening (low urine orotic acid, normal serum citrulline and arginine). Serum cryptococcal antigen titer was >1:2560.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission lumbar puncture revealed opening pressure of 8 cmH2O (rising on repeat LPs to >45 cmH2O), encapsulated yeast on CSF Gram stain, CSF cryptococcal antigen titer >1:2560, and positive CSF, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), and blood cultures for Cryptococcus. Brain MRI showed no cytotoxic cerebral edema; abdominal imaging showed progressive splenic infarcts with necrosis requiring splenectomy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of early post-liver transplant disseminated cryptococcosis (meningitis, pneumonia, fungemia, and splenic infarcts) presenting with severe non-cirrhotic hyperammonemia (peak 692 umol/L), confirmed by CSF Gram stain, serum and CSF CrAg titers >1:2560, and positive blood, BAL, and CSF fungal cultures. Treated with IV liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), lactulose, rifaximin, zinc, empiric doxycycline, IV ganciclovir, and every-48-hour large-volume therapeutic lumbar punctures (as severe thrombocytopenia of 16 x 10^3/uL precluded permanent CSF shunting). Despite fungal culture clearance and ammonia normalization, persistent microvascular sludging caused refractory hydrocephalus, oliguric renal failure, splenic necrosis (requiring splenectomy), duodenal leak, and sepsis, and he was transitioned to hospice care.
